test.title: Giving old clothes a new life

paragraphs.text: Every year, millions of tonnes of clothing are thrown away in Europe, and less than one per cent of the material is made into new clothes. Most textiles end up in landfill or are burned.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: One obstacle is that many garments are made from blends of fibres, such as cotton mixed with polyester. These are difficult to separate, and most recycling machines can process only a single type of fibre.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: A Swedish company has developed a process that uses heat and water to separate cotton from polyester. The recovered cotton is turned into pulp and then into new fibre, while the polyester can be melted and reused.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Second-hand shops also play a part. However, charities report that the quality of donated clothes has fallen, because cheaper garments wear out quickly and are often too damaged to sell.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Some governments now require clothing brands to pay for collecting and recycling the garments they sell. Supporters say this will encourage companies to design clothes that last longer and are easier to recycle.
paragraphs.label: E
